planting.note: Divide or transplant in spring once soil has warmed, siting in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil.

directions: This white sport of pink turtlehead retains the species' preference for damp streambanks and rain-garden edges, tolerating standing moisture better than most perennials. Grow in dappled to fairly deep shade with rich, evenly moist soil; full sun is workable only if roots never dry out. Pinching stems back in late spring encourages bushier, more floriferous growth by the late-summer bloom period. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor and flower count.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set out divisions or nursery plants in spring in reliably moist, fertile soil for best bottlebrush bloom display.

directions: This East Asian burnet produces long, drooping bottlebrush flower spikes above finely cut foliage, making it a graceful choice for bog gardens and pond margins. It prefers consistently moist to wet soil and benefits from light afternoon shade in hotter climates to prevent leaf scorch. Stake taller stems in exposed sites, since the arching flower spikes can lodge in wind and rain. Established clumps can be divided in spring every three to four years to refresh vigor.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes
American Horticultural Society A-Z Encyclopedia of Garden Plants

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich soil where the pendant white spikes can be appreciated up close.

directions: The white-flowered form of Japanese burnet carries the same drooping bottlebrush habit as the species but with pale, almost luminous spikes that show well against dark backdrops. It performs best in evenly moist soil with morning sun and afternoon shade, particularly in warmer zones. Deadhead spent spikes to tidy the planting, though they can also be left for subtle winter interest. Divide every few years in early spring once the crown becomes crowded.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Purpurea Japanese Burnet (Deep Purple-Red Bottlebrush Burnet)

planting.note: Plant in spring in fertile, consistently moist soil; the deep wine-purple spikes are a strong late-summer accent.

directions: This selection produces long, nodding spikes in a rich purple-red that darkens further in cooler autumn weather, contrasting nicely with ornamental grasses in a moist border. Keep soil evenly damp and provide some afternoon shade where summers run hot to preserve flower color and prevent stress. The airy, fine-textured foliage benefits from a spring cutback of old growth before new shoots emerge. Divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep the display full.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes
American Horticultural Society A-Z Encyclopedia of Garden Plants

planting.note: Set out transplants after the danger of hard frost, in full sun with reliably moist soil for the sturdiest stems.

directions: 'Snowbank' is the classic compact selection of native false aster, prized for staying self-supporting even when smothered in small white daisies from late summer into fall. It thrives in moist to average garden soil and, unlike the straight species, rarely needs staking. Cutting stems back by a third in early summer produces a bushier, more floriferous plant at bloom time. Divide every two to three years in spring, since clumps spread and can decline in vigor at the center.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Pink Beauty Boltonia (Soft Pink False Aster)

planting.note: Transplant in spring into moist, fertile soil in full sun to encourage full, well-branched flowering stems.

directions: This soft pink-flowered selection brings warmer color to the typically white-flowered native false aster while keeping the same airy, cloud-like bloom effect in late summer and fall. Grow in evenly moist soil and full sun for the densest flowering and to minimize floppy growth. A midseason pinch or light shear helps control height and encourages branching for more bloom stems. Divide every few years in spring to keep clumps vigorous and prevent overcrowding.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Honeysong Purple Stokes' Aster (Deep Violet-Purple Selection)

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained but consistently moist soil; good drainage in winter is essential for this evergreen native.

directions: 'Honeysong Purple' produces large, fringed, deep violet-purple daisy-like blooms on a compact clump of glossy evergreen leaves native to the southeastern coastal plain. It wants full sun and soil that stays on the moist side during the growing season but drains well in winter, since soggy crowns in cold weather are its main weakness. Deadheading spent flowers extends the summer bloom season considerably. Mulch lightly in colder zones to protect the evergreen rosette, and divide overgrown clumps in early spring.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
